etymologies.etymologyHTML: From bank +‎ -er, after French banquier.

definitions.definition: One who conducts the business of banking; one who, individually, or as a member of a company, keeps an establishment for the deposit or loan of money, or for traffic in money, bills of exchange, etc.

quote.citation: 1855 December – 1857 June, Charles Dickens, Little Dorrit, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1857, →OCLC:
quote.text: I have a good banker in this city, but I would not wish to draw upon the house until the time when I shall draw for a round sum.

definitions.definition: The dealer in a casino, or one who keeps the bank in a banking game.
The stone bench on which a mason cuts or squares his work.[1]

quote.citation: 1895, Thomas Hardy, “II-ii”, in Jude the Obscure, London: Osgood:
quote.text: [T]he new traceries, mullions, transoms, shafts, pinnacles, and battlements standing on the bankers half worked[.]

definitions.definition: (stationery) A type of envelope with a diamond shape or V-flap that opens on the long edge.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From bank (“an elevation, or rising ground”) +‎ -er (relational noun suffix) or +‎ -er (occupational suffix).

definitions.definition: A vessel employed in the cod fishery on the banks of Newfoundland.

quote.citation: May 20 1815, John Quincy Adams, letter to a merchant
quote.text: I think the 584 Bankers may be put down 36,540 tons, navigated by 4,627 men and boys

definitions.definition: (UK, dialect) A ditcher; a drain digger.

quote.citation: 1941, Ernestine Hill, My Love Must Wait, A&R Classics, published 2013, page 6:
quote.text: But this was no storm, the bankers could have told him. It was break of the year.

definitions.definition: (Australia, colloquial) A watercourse filled from bank to bank.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From bank (“an incline or hill”) +‎ -er.

definitions.definition: (rail transport, British, Australia) A railway locomotive that can be attached to the rear of a train to assist it in climbing an incline.

quote.citation: 1944 January and February, W. McGowan Gradon, “Forres as a Railway Centre”, in Railway Magazine, page 23:
quote.text: Between them these engines work passenger trains on the Keith line, and also act as bankers up to Dava when required.

quote.citation: 1960 May, “Motive Power Miscellany: Southern Region”, in Trains Illustrated, page 314:
quote.text: Because of a shortage of W.R. pannier tanks, two "E6" 0-6-2 tanks, Nos. 32410/5, were engaged as bankers on the Folkestone Harbour branch at the beginning of March; [...].
